questions.title: Why Checking 'Mandatory' on a Dictionary Entry Changes Every Form Instantly
questions.prompt: A junior admin asks you why checking the Mandatory checkbox on one dictionary entry for a custom field immediately enforces that field as required on every form built against that table -- including forms built after today -- without anyone writing a validation script or deploying code. Explain the underlying mechanism.
questions.modelAnswer: A dictionary entry on sys_dictionary isn't documentation of a field -- it IS the field, and ServiceNow reads that record live on every render rather than consulting a compiled schema. The Mandatory checkbox is just another column on that same sys_dictionary row, so the instant you save it, every form the platform renders against that table -- Agent Workspace, classic UI, and any form built tomorrow -- reads the current state of that row and enforces the red-border validation and save block automatically. No separate validation rule has to exist because there was never a separate schema file to update; the behavior and the configuration are the same data.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk them through the idea that ServiceNow doesn't compile a schema the way a hand-coded app does -- every field's behavior is read live from sys_dictionary on every page render. So checking Mandatory and saving isn't 'triggering' anything; it's just changing the one row the platform was already going to read the next time any form against that table loads. That's also why it applies to forms that don't exist yet: there's no list of forms to go update, because every form queries the same live dictionary record at render time.
commonMistakes: Assuming a UI Policy or Business Rule has to be written to enforce it
Thinking there's a cache that needs to be cleared or a restart required
Confusing the dictionary-level Mandatory flag (table-wide, always on) with a UI Policy's per-form conditional mandatory, which only applies on specific views under specific conditions
keyPoints: sys_dictionary record IS the field's definition, not documentation of it
The platform reads dictionary attributes live on every render
Mandatory applies platform-wide and to future forms with no extra deployment
This is distinct from a UI Policy's form-specific, conditional mandatory behavior

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies sys_dictionary as the live source of field behavior
Explains why no code/deployment is needed for the change to take effect
Distinguishes dictionary-level Mandatory from a UI Policy's form-specific mandatory

lessonLink.label: Review: The Dictionary & What It Controls

questions.title: Why Three ACLs on One Field Can All Need to Pass
questions.prompt: Explain how ServiceNow evaluates access when multiple ACLs apply to the same read attempt on a field, and why a new, narrower ACL added to tighten security on that field can break access that used to work for unrelated users.
questions.modelAnswer: Every ACL lives on sys_security_acl, and when more than one applicable ACL governs the same operation on the same record or field, ServiceNow evaluates them as an AND, not an OR -- every single applicable ACL has to pass for access to be granted. One failing ACL is enough to block the operation regardless of how many others would have allowed it. So adding a new, narrower ACL never weakens what already existed, but it adds one more rule to that AND chain, which can absolutely break access that previously worked for users who now fail the new rule even though they still pass every other ACL that applied before.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the one ACL fact that trips up almost every new admin, so I always say it explicitly: it's AND across every applicable ACL, never OR. If someone tells me access 'used to work' after they added an unrelated-seeming rule, my first question is whether they just added a new ACL to the same table or field, because that's almost always the real cause -- they added one more hurdle to a chain that already existed, and an existing user who passed everything before now fails the new one.
commonMistakes: Assuming access is granted if a user matches ANY applicable ACL
Not realizing a new, narrower ACL can break previously-working access for unrelated users
Treating table-level and field-level ACLs as alternatives instead of both being required
keyPoints: sys_security_acl holds every ACL on the instance
Every applicable ACL must pass -- it's an AND, not an OR
A single failing ACL blocks access regardless of how many others pass
Adding a new ACL can break existing access by adding one more AND condition

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states the AND evaluation rule across applicable ACLs
Explains why a new ACL can break previously-working access
Mentions sys_security_acl as where every ACL lives

lessonLink.label: Review: How ACLs Actually Evaluate Access

questions.title: What Actually Lands Inside an Update Set -- and What Never Does
questions.prompt: An admin creates a Business Rule and, in the same session, also closes ten test Incidents. Explain which of those two kinds of changes get captured inside the currently active Update Set, and why ServiceNow deliberately draws that line.
questions.modelAnswer: The new Business Rule gets captured, as a row on sys_update_xml inside the active Update Set (sys_update_set); the ten closed Incidents never do, no matter how long the Update Set stays active. The line ServiceNow draws is configuration/metadata versus data: Update Sets capture changes to how the platform is defined -- Business Rules, ACLs, dictionary entries, form layouts, Script Includes -- but never ordinary record changes like a new Incident or a state update. That boundary exists specifically so promoting a Business Rule to Production only ever changes behavior, never drags along Dev's throwaway test data as a side effect.
questions.professionalAnswer: I tell people to think of it as 'how the system behaves' versus 'the data inside it.' A Business Rule is part of the system's behavior, so it's captured. Closing ten test Incidents is just data changing state, so it's never captured, full stop, regardless of whether an Update Set happens to be active. If I need to move actual data between instances, that's an Import Set or Data Source's job, not an Update Set's.
commonMistakes: Assuming any change made while an Update Set is active gets captured
Confusing moving data between instances with promoting configuration
Not realizing the boundary is deliberate, not an accidental platform limitation
keyPoints: Update Sets capture configuration/metadata, never ordinary data records
sys_update_xml holds each individual captured change inside the set
A new Incident or closed ticket is never captured regardless of Update Set state
The boundary exists so promotion never silently drags along throwaway Dev data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates configuration/metadata from data records
Names sys_update_set / sys_update_xml correctly
Explains why this boundary is deliberate

lessonLink.label: Review: What an Update Set Actually Captures

questions.title: Proving 'Incident' Is Just a Row Somewhere in the System
questions.prompt: A coworker insists the Incident table must be special, hard-coded database structure unlike anything a custom table could be. Which table would you open to prove it's just a row like any other, and what specific attributes would you expect to find there?
questions.modelAnswer: Open sys_db_object and filter for the incident table -- it's one ordinary row there, carrying the real database name, the human-readable label, which table it extends, and whether it's extendable, exactly like any custom table's row in the same table. To go further, sys_dictionary holds one record per field on incident, the same way it does for any custom table's columns. There's no separate schema file anywhere that makes incident special; System Definition > Tables is literally a list view built directly on sys_db_object.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd just open System Definition > Tables with them, find Incident in the list, and point out it's one row among thousands, admin tables and custom tables included. Then I'd click into its Columns related list, which is really just sys_dictionary filtered to that table, and show that short_description's field definition looks structurally identical to a field on a table they built last week. Nothing about Incident's underlying representation is architecturally different -- it's just a table that happened to ship with the product.
commonMistakes: Assuming core ITSM tables like incident use a different underlying mechanism than custom tables
Not knowing sys_db_object is the actual 'table of tables'
Confusing sys_dictionary (fields) with sys_db_object (tables)

sys_dictionary holds one record per field, across every table
Incident's row looks structurally identical to a custom table's row
System Definition > Tables is a list view built directly on sys_db_object

questions.title: Why CSDM Exists Even Though You Don't 'Turn It On'
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks why your team should adopt CSDM for CMDB modeling instead of inventing its own structure for services, applications, and CIs, since CSDM isn't a feature you install. Explain the real problem CSDM solves and the cost of not adopting a shared model.
questions.modelAnswer: CSDM is a published, vendor-maintained reference framework for how CIs, applications, and services should relate -- documentation and a recommended structure, not a checkbox. Before a standard model existed, every implementation team made its own judgment calls about how to represent 'this is a service' or 'this is an application,' which meant data shaped for ITSM's expectations often didn't match what Service Portfolio Management needed, so dashboards built for one module misread or failed to find records meant for another. Adopting CSDM gives every module and every implementer a shared vocabulary to read and write against instead of a bespoke, one-off model that only one team understands.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it as the cost of NOT standardizing: without CSDM, every module -- ITSM, ITOM, Service Portfolio Management -- grows its own expectations for what a 'service' record looks like, and every implementer re-derives their own structure from scratch. That means lessons learned on one engagement don't transfer to the next, and a new admin has to relearn a bespoke model every time they join a different instance. CSDM isn't extra work layered on top of CMDB -- it's the thing that makes CMDB data usable by more than one person and more than one module at once.
commonMistakes: Treating CSDM as an installable feature rather than a reference framework
Underestimating the real cost of inconsistent service/application modeling across modules
Assuming CSDM only matters for ITOM, not ITSM and Service Portfolio Management too
keyPoints: CSDM is a documented reference framework, not a feature to enable
It solves the problem of every module/implementer inventing its own service model
Without it, data shaped for one module can misread or fail in another
CSDM gives ITSM, ITOM, and SPM a shared vocabulary to read and write against

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames CSDM as a reference framework, not a feature
Explains the real cost of inconsistent modeling across modules
Names at least two consumers of the shared model (e.g., ITSM, ITOM, SPM)

questions.title: Identification Rule Passing, Reconciliation Rule Still Producing Wrong Data
questions.prompt: A server's Identification Rule is correctly recognizing every incoming Discovery scan and manual import as the same CI -- no duplicates are being created. Yet the CI's OS Version field keeps getting overwritten with stale values from an old manual import. Explain why the Identification Rule working correctly doesn't protect against this, and what's actually missing.
questions.modelAnswer: Identification and Reconciliation solve two different problems. The Identification Rule only decides whether two incoming records describe the same real-world asset -- it's working fine here, since both sources are correctly landing on one CI. What's missing is a Reconciliation Rule, which decides which source's value wins per field when sources disagree. Without one, the CMDB falls back on the dangerous default of 'whichever source wrote last wins,' which lets a stale manual import silently overwrite a fresher, more accurate Discovery-reported OS version.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain that these are genuinely two separate rule types solving two separate questions: Identification asks 'is this the same CI,' and Reconciliation asks 'whose answer do I trust for this field.' A correct Identification Rule can't substitute for a missing Reconciliation Rule -- they don't overlap. The fix is designating Discovery as the authoritative source for OS Version specifically, since it inspects the actual running machine, while leaving fields Discovery can't observe, like Business Owner, authoritative from manual entry instead.
commonMistakes: Assuming a working Identification Rule also protects field-level data accuracy
Defaulting to 'most recent write wins' without an explicit Reconciliation Rule
Not realizing authoritative source should be designated per field, not per CI class as a whole
keyPoints: Identification Rules decide whether two records are the same CI
Reconciliation Rules decide which source wins on a specific field
The two rule types solve different problems and can't substitute for each other
Authoritative source should be set per field based on which source can actually observe it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes Identification from Reconciliation
Explains why 'most recent write wins' is a dangerous default
Proposes a field-specific authoritative source fix

questions.title: Where the Password Actually Lives in a SAML Login
questions.prompt: Walk through the SAML-based SSO login flow step by step and identify precisely which step involves the user's actual password, and which step ServiceNow uses to verify the login was legitimate.
questions.modelAnswer: The password lives entirely at Step 3 -- the user authenticates at the Identity Provider, with whatever password or MFA the IdP enforces. ServiceNow, as the Service Provider, never receives that password at any point in the flow. ServiceNow verifies the login at Step 6, when it validates the signature on the SAML assertion the browser carried back, checking it against the IdP's signing certificate stored in the Multi-Provider SSO configuration record. That cryptographic verification, not blind trust, is what actually confirms the assertion really came from the trusted IdP.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk it step by step: the browser is redirected to the IdP, the user authenticates there, the IdP builds and signs an assertion, the browser carries it back, and ServiceNow validates that signature against the certificate it has on file. The password only ever exists in that one step at the IdP -- ServiceNow's whole job is verifying a signed document, not collecting a credential. That's exactly why a SAML login failure almost always traces back to either an expired/mismatched signing certificate or a misconfigured entity ID/endpoint, not a password problem.
commonMistakes: Assuming ServiceNow receives or checks the password at some point
Not knowing which configuration record holds the IdP's signing certificate
Describing SAML trust as implicit rather than cryptographically verified
keyPoints: ServiceNow is the Service Provider; a separate system is the Identity Provider
The password is handled entirely at the IdP, in step 3 of the flow
ServiceNow verifies the assertion's signature, never the password itself
The Multi-Provider SSO configuration record holds the entity ID, SSO endpoint, and signing certificate

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the step where the password is handled
Correctly identifies the signature-verification step
Names the Multi-Provider SSO configuration record and its contents

questions.title: Client Credentials vs. Authorization Code for an Unattended Nightly Sync
questions.prompt: Your team is building a nightly, unattended job that pulls vendor data into ServiceNow with no human involved. Explain which OAuth 2.0 grant type is appropriate and why Authorization Code grant would be the wrong choice here.
questions.modelAnswer: Client Credentials grant is correct here: the integration authenticates as itself, using only its client ID and client secret, with no human user involved at all -- exactly the shape of a nightly, unattended job. Authorization Code grant would be wrong because it's designed for acting on behalf of a specific human user who has explicitly consented, requiring a one-time interactive consent step with the provider -- there's no human in a 3 AM scheduled job to perform that consent. Once an OAuth Entity Profile using Client Credentials is attached to the REST Message's Authentication Profile, ServiceNow also handles requesting, caching, and refreshing the token automatically.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ask one question first: is there a specific human's permissions this call needs to carry? If not, it's Client Credentials, full stop -- the integration presents its own identity and gets a token back. Authorization Code only makes sense when a real user needs to authorize access to something scoped to them personally, like their own calendar, which requires an interactive consent step nobody's around to click at 3 AM. And once it's wired up, I don't manage token expiry in script at all -- ServiceNow caches and refreshes it for me.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to Authorization Code because it 'sounds more secure'
Not realizing Authorization Code requires a human consent step that can't happen unattended
Manually tracking token expiry in script instead of letting the OAuth Entity Profile handle it
keyPoints: Client Credentials grant: the integration authenticates as itself, no human involved
Authorization Code grant: requires a human's explicit, interactive consent
An unattended nightly job has no human available to perform that consent
ServiceNow automatically requests, caches, and refreshes the token once configured

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly selects Client Credentials grant for the scenario
Correctly explains why Authorization Code doesn't fit
Mentions ServiceNow's automatic token lifecycle handling

questions.title: Candidate vs. Declared: Why a Major Incident Isn't Automatic
questions.prompt: Your organization's Priority 1 incident volume has grown, and someone proposes auto-declaring any Priority 1 incident as a Major Incident to save time. Explain why major_incident_state is modeled with a Candidate step before Declared, and what breaks if that step is skipped.
questions.modelAnswer: major_incident_state keeps None, Candidate, and Declared as distinct values specifically so hitting a severity threshold surfaces an incident for human review rather than automatically spinning up the full MIM apparatus. If Candidate were skipped and every threshold-crossing Priority 1 auto-Declared, false positives become common -- a Priority 1 affecting one VIP user, correctly handled by a normal incident process, would still trigger a war room, bridge calls, and a fixed communication cadence it never needed. That erodes trust in the MIM process the first time it fires for something that clearly didn't warrant it, and people start ignoring Major Incident alerts altogether.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on auto-declaration directly: the Candidate state exists precisely to put a human -- usually a major incident manager or on-call lead -- in the loop before the heavier process spins up. Skip that and you WILL get false positives, because Priority alone doesn't capture real business severity. And the real cost isn't just wasted war-room time; it's that the next time MIM genuinely fires, people have already learned to tune it out because it cried wolf before.
commonMistakes: Treating Priority 1 and Major Incident as automatically the same thing
Assuming automatic declaration is strictly more efficient than a human review step
Not anticipating the trust-erosion cost of false-positive Major Incident declarations
keyPoints: major_incident_state has None, Candidate, and Declared as distinct values
Candidate surfaces for human review; Declared confirms the MIM process is active
Automatic declaration produces false positives that erode trust in the process
A human decision-maker is what separates MIM from the ordinary incident lifecycle

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the Candidate vs. Declared distinction
Explains the false-positive risk of automatic declaration
Connects this to the human decision-maker's role

questions.title: Why a 4-Hour SLA Started at 4 PM Friday Doesn't Breach at 8 PM
questions.prompt: An SLA Definition targets 4 business hours and uses an 8-5 Weekdays schedule. Explain why an incident opened at 4:00 PM on a Friday doesn't breach at 8:00 PM the same day, and what would change if no schedule were attached to the definition at all.
questions.modelAnswer: SLA duration math is schedule-aware, not a flat 24/7 countdown. With an 8-5 Weekdays schedule attached, the task_sla instance only accumulates elapsed time during the hours that schedule defines as business hours, so it counts 1 hour on Friday (4-5 PM), pauses for the entire weekend, and resumes Monday morning, breaching around noon Monday once the remaining 3 hours elapse. If no schedule were attached, the SLA would run 24/7, and 4 business hours from 4 PM Friday would simply be 8 PM Friday -- a completely different real-world deadline for the same 'duration' number.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the detail that trips people up when they're staring at a duration field and assuming it's wall-clock time. I'd point to the cmn_schedule record attached to the SLA Definition and explain that '4 hours' only means something once you know which hours count. With 8-5 Weekdays attached, the clock genuinely pauses outside business hours and over the weekend; strip the schedule off entirely and you get a 24/7 countdown instead, which is the right call for some Priority 1 definitions but dead wrong for anything meant to only count business hours.
commonMistakes: Assuming SLA duration is always a flat wall-clock countdown
Not checking which cmn_schedule record, if any, is attached to the SLA Definition
Treating a missing schedule as an oversight rather than a deliberate (sometimes wrong) choice
keyPoints: SLA duration math is schedule-aware via a cmn_schedule record like '8-5 Weekdays'
The clock pauses outside the defined business hours and over weekends/holidays
No schedule attached means the SLA runs 24/7 instead
The same 'duration' number means a different real deadline depending on the schedule

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes the Monday-noon breach time with the schedule applied
Explains what changes with no schedule attached
Names cmn_schedule as the mechanism

lessonLink.label: Review: SLA Workflows: Pause, Stop, Breach

questions.title: Why current Inside a Business Rule Can Touch Data the User Can't See
questions.prompt: Explain why a Business Rule running on the Incident table can read and write a completely unrelated custom table, including data the logged-in user isn't permitted to see through the UI, and why that makes Business Rules more dangerous than a UI Policy.
questions.modelAnswer: A Business Rule is a sys_script record that runs on the ServiceNow application server, inside the same transaction as the database write, with full GlideRecord access to any table -- not just the one the user is looking at, and not constrained by the logged-in user's own role or ACLs. That server-side reach is exactly why it can query sys_user, update change_request, or write to an unrelated custom table, all before or after one Incident save finishes, with no sandboxing by default. A UI Policy, by contrast, only runs in the browser and can only hide or require a field on a form -- it has no path to touch data at all, which is why a careless Business Rule is a categorically bigger risk.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd draw the line at where each one executes: a UI Policy runs client-side and can only affect what's visible or required on a form in front of one user. A Business Rule runs server-side, inside the save transaction, with the same unrestricted GlideRecord access any developer script has -- it isn't filtered by the user's own permissions. That's the whole reason I treat every Business Rule as production code the moment I activate it, because it can rewrite data across the entire instance, silently, on every matching save.
commonMistakes: Assuming server-side scripts are constrained by the logged-in user's own ACLs
Treating Business Rules and UI Policies as similar-risk mechanisms
Not realizing a Business Rule can touch tables completely unrelated to the one it's defined on
keyPoints: Business Rules run server-side, inside the same transaction as the database write
They have full GlideRecord access to any table, not filtered by the user's own role
A UI Policy, by contrast, only runs client-side and can only affect form visibility/requirement
No sandboxing by default means a careless Business Rule is an instance-wide risk

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains server-side execution and unrestricted GlideRecord access
Contrasts this clearly with a UI Policy's limited, client-side scope
Names sys_script as where Business Rules live

lessonLink.label: Review: What a Business Rule Actually Is

questions.title: GlideRecord Is a Cursor, Not a Loaded Copy of the Data
questions.prompt: A new developer assumes new GlideRecord('incident') immediately loads every incident into memory. Correct that assumption precisely, and explain what current actually is inside a Business Rule.
questions.modelAnswer: new GlideRecord('incident') doesn't fetch a single row -- it creates a cursor object positioned over the incident table's schema, capable of pointing at zero, one, or many rows, but nothing happens against the database until .query() or .get() is explicitly called. current, inside a Business Rule, is literally a GlideRecord object of exactly this type, except the platform has already queried it and positioned it on the one record being inserted, updated, or deleted -- you didn't write new GlideRecord(...) yourself, but current behaves identically to one you had.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct it immediately: that line alone does zero database work. It's a cursor, not a result set -- think of it as an object that knows how to ask the incident table questions, not a snapshot of every incident. And current is the exact same kind of object, just handed to you already positioned on the triggering record, which is why everything you learn about reading and setting fields with a GlideRecord you create yourself applies directly to current with no translation needed.
commonMistakes: Believing new GlideRecord(table) loads all matching rows into memory immediately
Not realizing .query() or .get() is what actually triggers database work
Treating current as a special object type different from an ordinary GlideRecord
keyPoints: GlideRecord is a cursor positioned over a table, not a loaded dataset
No database work happens until .query() or .get() is called
current inside a Business Rule is a GlideRecord already positioned on the triggering record
Everything learned about an ordinary GlideRecord applies directly to current

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly corrects the 'loads everything into memory' assumption
Explains .query()/.get() as the actual trigger for database work
Correctly identifies current as an already-positioned GlideRecord

questions.title: Why Two Scoped Apps Can Both Have a Table Named 'Request'
questions.prompt: Two unrelated scoped applications, x_acme_fleet and x_acme_vms, each want a table they think of as 'Request.' Explain why this never collides, and what the real table name looks like for each.
questions.modelAnswer: Every scoped application gets its own sys_scope record defining a distinct namespace, and when a table is created inside that scope, ServiceNow automatically prefixes its real database name with the scope identifier. So a table named 'Request' inside x_acme_fleet really becomes x_acme_fleet_request, while the same conceptual table inside x_acme_vms becomes x_acme_vms_request -- two entirely distinct tables that never collide, because the scope boundary is enforced by the platform's naming mechanism itself, not by developers remembering a convention.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out that the collision is impossible by construction, not by discipline -- the scope identifier gets baked directly into the real table name the moment the table is created, so x_acme_fleet's 'Request' and x_acme_vms's 'Request' are never actually the same string in the database. This is exactly the problem scope was built to solve: in the old Global-only world, two teams both naming a table 'Request' really would collide or silently overwrite each other.
commonMistakes: Assuming naming collisions are avoided by convention rather than platform enforcement
Not knowing the scope identifier is baked directly into the real table name
Confusing the Global scope's lack of isolation with how scoped applications behave
keyPoints: Each scoped application has its own sys_scope record defining an isolated namespace
Table names are automatically prefixed with the scope identifier (e.g. x_acme_fleet_request)
This makes naming collisions impossible by construction, not convention
The same prefixing applies to Script Includes and most other scriptable artifacts

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains automatic scope-identifier prefixing
Gives the correct real table names for both scopes
Explains why this is platform-enforced, not convention-based

questions.title: Writing the GlideAjax Round Trip for a Client-Side Duplicate Check
questions.prompt: A catalog item's client script needs to check, before the user submits, whether a typed asset tag already exists in the alm_asset table -- without giving the browser direct GlideRecord access. Write the Script Include method and the calling Client Script that make this check happen safely.
questions.modelAnswer: The Client Script never touches alm_asset directly -- it calls GlideAjax against a Script Include method, which is the only place GlideRecord is allowed to run. AssetTagChecker.tagExists() reads the parameter, runs a limited GlideRecord query server-side, and returns a plain string result; the Client Script's callback receives that result asynchronously and shows or hides a field message based on it. Nothing in the browser ever issues a database query -- it only ever asks a pre-approved question and waits for an answer.
questions.professionalAnswer: I build this the same way every time: a small, single-purpose Script Include method that does exactly one thing server-side, called through GlideAjax from the client script, with the result handled in a callback because the call is asynchronous. I'd also flag that getXMLAnswer's callback doesn't run on the next line -- it runs whenever the server actually responds, so I never structure logic that assumes the answer is ready immediately after the GlideAjax call.
questions.example: Typing an asset tag that already exists in alm_asset triggers the onChange handler, which calls AssetTagChecker.tagExists() through GlideAjax and shows a field error message once the async callback returns 'true'.
commonMistakes: Trying to reference GlideRecord directly inside a Client Script
Assuming the GlideAjax result is available on the line right after the call, ignoring the async callback
Forgetting setLimit(1) on the Script Include query, scanning more rows than needed for a yes/no check
keyPoints: Client Scripts can never call GlideRecord directly -- only GlideAjax to a Script Include
The Script Include method does the real database work and returns a plain value
The round trip is asynchronous; the callback runs later, not on the next line
setLimit(1) keeps a yes/no existence check cheap

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Script Include correctly queries alm_asset and returns a plain value
Client Script correctly calls GlideAjax and handles the async callback

questions.title: Fixing an N+1 GlideRecord Query Inside a Loop
questions.prompt: The following script counts open incidents per company by querying inside a loop over every company. Rewrite it so it issues exactly one query against incident regardless of how many companies exist.
questions.modelAnswer: Replace the per-company query with one single query against incident, then group the results in memory with a plain JavaScript object keyed by company sys_id. One query total, no matter how many companies exist, because the N+1 pattern -- one query to get N rows plus N more queries inside the loop -- is exactly what's being eliminated.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd flag the structure immediately: a GlideRecord query inside a while loop over another GlideRecord is the single most damaging pattern in this course, because it scales with the outer loop's row count instead of staying flat. The fix is always the same shape -- pull everything you need in one query, then tally or look things up in memory with a plain object instead of asking the database again for each row.
commonMistakes: Not recognizing the query-inside-a-loop pattern as N+1
Assuming the fix requires a more complex query instead of simply moving the query outside the loop
Forgetting to key the in-memory tally by the right field (company sys_id)
keyPoints: A query inside a loop over N rows produces N+1 total queries
The fix moves the second query outside the loop entirely
Grouping/counting happens in memory with a plain JavaScript object
This stays exactly one query regardless of how many companies exist

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the N+1 pattern in the original code
Rewrites it as exactly one query against incident
Correctly implements in-memory grouping/counting

questions.title: Building an Idempotent, Backoff-Protected Webhook Handler for External Alerts
questions.prompt: Design and implement a scripted REST endpoint that receives alert webhooks from an external monitoring tool and creates ServiceNow incidents from them. The external tool retries on any non-200 response, sometimes sending the same alert two or three times. Build the handler so retries never create duplicate incidents, and show how you'd call a flaky downstream system safely from within the same transaction.

deepDive.heading: The duplicate-record risk
deepDive.content: If the webhook handler blindly inserts a new incident every time it receives a payload, a retried request -- caused by a lost response rather than a real failure on the first attempt -- creates a second incident record for the same underlying alert. The external tool can't tell the difference between 'my request never arrived' and 'it arrived but the response got lost,' so it will retry on both, and the handler has to be the one that absorbs that ambiguity safely.

deepDive.heading: Coalesce field and upsert pattern
deepDive.content: The fix is a coalesce field: a custom field like u_external_alert_id that stores the external system's unique alert ID. Before inserting, the handler queries incident for an existing record with that external ID. If one exists, this is a retry (or a duplicate webhook) and the handler updates it instead of inserting a second one. If none exists, it's genuinely the first time this alert has been seen, and a new incident is created and stamped with that external ID. Running the handler once, or three times because the first two responses timed out, produces exactly one incident record either way.

deepDive.heading: Calling a flaky downstream system safely
deepDive.content: If the handler itself needs to call another system (for example, to enrich the alert with asset data) before finishing, that call should use exponential backoff rather than retrying immediately or at a fixed interval: wait 1 second, then 2, then 4, doubling each time, using gs.sleep(ms) between attempts. This gives a struggling downstream system room to recover and avoids every retrying caller hammering it in lockstep.

deepDive.heading: Putting it together
What this doesn't solve
deepDive.content: The coalesce-field pattern guarantees exactly one incident per external alert ID, but it does NOT guarantee the fields on that incident reflect the most complete version of the data if two retries arrive with genuinely different payloads for the same alert ID -- that's a reconciliation decision (which payload's fields should win) separate from the idempotency guarantee itself, and should be made explicit in the upsert logic rather than left to whichever retry happens to run last.

commonMistakes: Inserting a new incident on every webhook call with no coalesce check
Retrying a downstream call immediately or at a fixed interval instead of backing off exponentially
Treating 'idempotent' as meaning 'safe to ignore retries' rather than 'safe to run more than once with the same end result'
keyPoints: A coalesce field (external alert ID) is what makes the create operation idempotent
Query-then-update-or-insert (upsert) is the standard pattern for this
Exponential backoff protects a struggling downstream system during retries
Idempotency and data reconciliation across retries are related but separate concerns

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements the coalesce-field upsert pattern
Correctly implements exponential backoff for the downstream call
Explains why idempotency prevents duplicate incidents under retry
Notes the limits of the idempotency guarantee re: data reconciliation

questions.title: Fixing a Business Rule That Triggers Itself Forever
questions.prompt: The following update-triggered Business Rule on Incident calls current.update() inside itself and is causing a recursion error. Rewrite it correctly, explaining why the fix works.
questions.modelAnswer: The fix is to add an idempotent guard and remove the redundant current.update() call entirely, since this is a Before-style field change: check whether the work_notes value would actually differ before touching it, and let the platform's own single save include the change -- there's no need to call current.update() a second time inside a Before rule at all, and doing so is exactly what re-triggers the same update rule. If the rule genuinely needs to run as an After rule and must explicitly save, current.setWorkflow(false) before that update prevents the save from re-firing business rules on the table.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd first ask whether this is configured as a Before or After rule, because the fix differs slightly. If it's Before, the real bug is calling current.update() at all -- Before-rule field changes are already included in the one save happening anyway, so deleting that line fixes it outright. If it has to be After, I'd keep the explicit update but call current.setWorkflow(false) first so that save doesn't re-trigger the rule, and I'd still add the idempotent guard so a run that would be a no-op never saves at all.
commonMistakes: Calling current.update() inside a Before rule, forcing a second, self-triggering save
Not adding an idempotent guard so an unnecessary save happens even when nothing changed
Forgetting current.setWorkflow(false) when an After rule genuinely must call current.update()
keyPoints: Before-rule field changes don't need an explicit current.update() call at all
current.update() inside an update-triggered rule re-triggers that same rule
current.setWorkflow(false) prevents a necessary After-rule save from re-firing rules
An idempotent guard skips the action entirely when nothing would actually change

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies current.update() as the root cause of the recursion
Provides a correct fix (removing the redundant call or using setWorkflow(false))
Adds or explains the idempotent guard

questions.title: Configuring a Change Advisory Board Approval That Requires Every Member
questions.prompt: A high-risk Normal change needs sign-off from every member of the Change Advisory Board -- a single rejection should stop the change, and the step shouldn't resolve until everyone has responded. Which Flow Designer Ask for Approval variant do you configure, and what record type does ServiceNow create behind the scenes for each board member?
questions.modelAnswer: Configure 'Approval from a group -- everyone,' pointed at the CAB group, not 'anyone,' because 'anyone' resolves as soon as a single member responds and would let one approver clear a decision meant to be collective. Behind the scenes, this creates a sysapproval_approver record for each group member; every one of those records has to reach a final approved state for the step to resolve, while a single rejection from any member closes the step out as rejected. The flow genuinely pauses at this step -- it isn't polling in a loop -- and only resumes once those approval records collectively reach a final state.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd configure 'group -- everyone' specifically because this is a genuinely collective decision, not a 'first qualified person to respond' situation -- 'anyone' would undermine the entire point of requiring the whole board's sign-off. I'd also make sure whoever reviews this flow knows that what's actually happening under the hood is a set of real sysapproval_approver records, the same ones that drive the ordinary Approvals module, so each board member sees this in their normal approvals list rather than through some flow-specific UI.
commonMistakes: Choosing 'group -- anyone' for a decision meant to require the full board's agreement
Not knowing sysapproval_approver is the real record type created per approver
Assuming the flow polls in a loop rather than genuinely pausing until the approval resolves
keyPoints: 'Group -- everyone' requires every member to approve; a single rejection closes the step
'Group -- anyone' resolves on the first response, which is wrong for a collective decision
Each approver gets a real sysapproval_approver record, visible in their own approvals list
The flow genuinely pauses execution, resuming only when the approval(s) reach a final state

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly selects 'group -- everyone' over 'group -- anyone'
Correctly names sysapproval_approver as the underlying record type
Explains that the flow genuinely pauses rather than polling

questions.title: Building a Shared 'Requester Info' Variable Set for Three Catalog Items
questions.prompt: New Laptop Request, Software Install, and Conference Room Booking all need to ask who the request is really for and which cost center to bill. Design the variable(s) and decide whether they belong on each item directly or inside a shared Variable Set, and justify your variable type choice.
questions.modelAnswer: Both 'Requested For' and 'Cost Center' should live inside one shared Variable Set, something like 'Requester Info,' attached to all three catalog items, because the exact same question is logically identical across all of them -- the test is that you'd otherwise be copying the same variable configuration by hand onto each item. 'Requested For' should be a Reference variable pointed at sys_user, not Single Line Text, so the answer is guaranteed to be a real, resolvable user record that downstream approvals and fulfillment workflows can act on, instead of a typed name with no guarantee it matches anything. 'Cost Center' is a Reference variable too, pointed at the cost center table, for the same reason: free text risks typos that break billing reconciliation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd group these into a shared Variable Set immediately, because the moment I'm tempted to copy a variable's configuration from one catalog item to the next by hand, that's the signal it belongs in a set instead -- fixing a typo or adding a new cost center choice later means editing one place, not three. And I'd insist on Reference variables for both fields rather than free text, because a Reference variable guarantees the requester picked an actual record your workflows can resolve, instead of typing something a human has to clean up later.
commonMistakes: Defining the same variables separately on each of the three catalog items
Using Single Line Text for 'Requested For' instead of a Reference variable pointed at sys_user
Not recognizing the 'would I be copying this by hand' test for when a variable belongs in a set
keyPoints: Variables logically identical across multiple items belong in a shared Variable Set
A Variable Set change propagates to every item using it immediately
Reference variables guarantee a resolvable record, unlike free text
The 'copying it by hand' test is the practical signal for when to use a set

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recommends a shared Variable Set over per-item definitions
Correctly chooses Reference variable type and justifies it
Articulates the practical test for when a variable belongs in a set

questions.title: Writing a Fast, Scripted ACL Condition for Group-Restricted Records
questions.prompt: Write the scripted condition for an ACL that should grant read access only to members of a specific group, and explain why your implementation is the standard, fast pattern rather than the common slow anti-pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: The fast pattern uses gs.getUser().isMemberOf('<group_sys_id>'), because GlideUser is already loaded once per transaction and cached, so this check costs nothing extra -- no fresh GlideRecord query runs against the database. The anti-pattern instead queries sys_user_grmember from scratch on every single access attempt to the governed record or field, and because ACL scripts run on every form load, every list view, every Table API call, and every report, that extra query multiplies across the entire instance's traffic, not just one transaction.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always reach for gs.getUser().isMemberOf() first for exactly this reason: ACL scripts aren't like a Business Rule that runs once per save -- they run on every single access attempt, so a 50ms query that would be invisible in a scheduled job becomes a real, measurable, instance-wide cost here. The GlideUser object already has the current user's roles and group memberships cached for the transaction, so this check is effectively free compared to a fresh query.
questions.example: A table-level ACL on incident.read with this scripted condition denies access instantly for any user not in the group, with no per-row database round trip beyond what GlideUser already cached for the transaction.
commonMistakes: Running a fresh GlideRecord query against sys_user_grmember inside the ACL script
Not recognizing that ACL scripts run on every access attempt, not once per transaction
Querying for data that's already available directly on current instead of reading it
keyPoints: gs.getUser().isMemberOf() checks cached group membership with no fresh query
ACL scripts run on every access attempt, so their cost compounds instance-wide
The sys_user_grmember query anti-pattern issues a real database round trip every time
Prefer data already available on current over querying to re-derive it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly writes the isMemberOf() pattern
Correctly identifies the anti-pattern and why it's slow
Explains why ACL script performance matters more than most script types

questions.title: Designing a Reusable Subflow for Standard Notification-and-Escalation
questions.prompt: Several unrelated flows need the exact same notification-and-escalation sequence. Design this as a Subflow: what inputs does it need to accept to stay generic across all the parent flows that will call it, and what should it return?
questions.modelAnswer: The Subflow should accept inputs for whatever varies across callers -- a record reference (so it knows what the notification is about), the group or user to notify, and an escalation threshold (how long to wait before escalating) -- rather than hard-coding any of those. It should return an output indicating the outcome, such as whether escalation actually fired, so a calling flow can branch on that result with ordinary If/Else logic afterward. Structurally it's still a sys_hub_flow record like any flow, just flagged as a subflow type and built to be called rather than triggered directly.
questions.professionalAnswer: I design subflow inputs around 'what would be different for every caller' -- here that's the record being escalated, who to notify, and the escalation window. Anything that's always the same across every call shouldn't be an input at all; it should just be built into the subflow's logic. On the output side, I always give the caller something to branch on afterward rather than a subflow that's a dead end, because otherwise every parent flow ends up duplicating its own ad hoc way of checking what happened.
commonMistakes: Hard-coding a specific group or threshold instead of exposing it as an input
Building a subflow with no output, leaving callers unable to branch on what happened
Forgetting a subflow is still a sys_hub_flow record, just flagged differently from a directly-triggered flow
keyPoints: Subflow inputs should cover everything that varies across callers
A subflow is called by other flows, not triggered directly, but is still a sys_hub_flow record
Outputs let the calling flow branch on the real outcome
Building once and reusing beats duplicating the same logic across multiple flows

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies sensible, generic inputs for the subflow
Defines a meaningful output the caller can branch on
Correctly describes the subflow-vs-flow structural relationship

questions.title: Writing a Service Portal Widget's Server Script to Power 'My Open Incidents'
questions.prompt: Build the Server Script for a Service Portal widget that shows the logged-in user's 10 most recent open incidents, and explain why you can't just hand the HTML Template a raw GlideRecord object.
questions.modelAnswer: The Server Script queries incident filtered to the current user's own records, capped with setLimit(10) and ordered by creation date, then pushes plain values -- via getValue() and getDisplayValue() -- into a data.incidents array, never the GlideRecord object itself. A raw GlideRecord can't cross from server script to client because the client only ever receives the plain data object the framework serializes; attempting to hand over the live GlideRecord would try to serialize a server-side cursor object the client-side AngularJS layer has no way to interact with.
questions.professionalAnswer: I build every widget's Server Script the same way: query exactly what I need, cap it with setLimit so I'm not pulling more than the widget will ever show, and push only plain strings/numbers into the data object. I never try to pass the GlideRecord itself across -- the HTML Template and Client Controller only ever see what's on data, and that has to already be plain, serializable values by the time the script finishes.
questions.example: data.incidents ends up as an array of plain objects like {number: 'INC0010045', short_description: 'VPN down', state: 'In Progress', sys_id: '...'}, which the HTML Template then loops over with ng-repeat.
commonMistakes: Trying to push the raw GlideRecord object itself into data instead of plain values
Forgetting setLimit(10), pulling every matching row before the widget only shows 10
Querying active incidents platform-wide instead of scoping to the current user's caller_id

Only plain values (strings, numbers, arrays of plain objects) can cross to the client
setLimit() and addQuery('caller_id', ...) correctly scope the query
getValue()/getDisplayValue() are what produce the plain values pushed into data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly scopes the query to the current user and active incidents
Correctly uses setLimit and orderByDesc
Explains why only plain values, not the GlideRecord itself, can cross to the client

questions.title: Building a Scripted REST API Endpoint for an External Partner
questions.prompt: A partner system needs to create ServiceNow Incidents through a REST call using a fixed JSON shape your company controls, rather than the generic Table API. Describe the Scripted REST API resource you'd build (method, relative path, and what the script body does), and explain why a Scripted REST API is the right choice over exposing the Table API directly here.
questions.modelAnswer: Build a POST resource on a Scripted REST API, something like /partner/incidents, whose script body reads the incoming request body against the partner's own fixed JSON shape, validates and translates those fields into the real incident field names, creates the record with GlideRecord, and returns a response in the partner's expected shape rather than ServiceNow's native Table API response format. This is the right choice over the Table API because it gives full control over the request/response contract, lets you validate and reject malformed partner payloads before they ever reach a GlideRecord insert, and decouples the partner's integration from ServiceNow's own internal field names, so a later field rename on incident doesn't break the partner's integration.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on exposing the Table API directly here because it ties the partner's contract directly to ServiceNow's own internal schema -- any field rename or structural change on our side becomes a breaking change for them. A Scripted REST API resource gives me a stable, versioned contract I control, where I can validate the partner's exact JSON shape, translate it into whatever the incident table actually needs, and return a response shaped the way the partner's system expects, independent of how our own data model evolves.
commonMistakes: Exposing the Table API directly and letting the partner depend on internal field names
Skipping request validation, letting malformed partner payloads hit GlideRecord directly
Not versioning the Scripted REST API resource, making future contract changes risky
keyPoints: A Scripted REST API resource defines its own request/response contract
It decouples the partner's integration from ServiceNow's internal field names
The script body validates and translates before touching GlideRecord
This is the right tool when a fixed, external-facing JSON shape is required

Explains the decoupling benefit over the Table API
Mentions request validation as part of the design

questions.title: Configuring a Field That's Mandatory on Insert But Read-Only After
questions.prompt: A custom field needs to be required when a record is first created, but locked from editing afterward. Can a single dictionary entry's Mandatory and Read-only flags alone achieve this, or do you need another mechanism too? Walk through your actual configuration.
questions.modelAnswer: No -- dictionary-level Mandatory and Read-only flags are static and apply the same way on every save, with no built-in concept of 'only on insert' versus 'only afterward.' Checking Read-only at the dictionary level would lock the field before it was ever set, and leaving it unchecked never locks it at all. The real configuration is a UI Policy (or Data Policy for server-side enforcement) with a condition based on whether the record is new -- apply Mandatory while the record is new, and apply Read-only once it isn't -- leaving the dictionary entry's own flags off entirely so the UI Policy is the only thing controlling this behavior.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct the assumption first: dictionary flags don't know about insert-vs-update, they're just always-on or always-off. The actual mechanism is a UI Policy scoped with a condition on the record being new, flipping Mandatory on for a new record and flipping Read-only on once it's saved -- and for server-side enforcement that can't be bypassed from the client, I'd back that same logic with a Data Policy too, rather than relying on the dictionary entry to do something it structurally can't.
commonMistakes: Assuming the dictionary entry's own flags can be conditional on insert vs. update
Checking Read-only at the dictionary level, which locks the field before it can ever be set
Relying only on a client-side UI Policy with no server-side Data Policy backing it
keyPoints: Dictionary-level Mandatory/Read-only flags are static, not insert-vs-update aware
A UI Policy conditioned on the record being new is the real mechanism for this
A Data Policy provides the equivalent server-side enforcement
The dictionary entry's own flags should be left off when a UI/Data Policy is driving this behavior

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states dictionary flags alone can't achieve insert-vs-update behavior
Correctly proposes a UI Policy conditioned on the record being new
Mentions Data Policy for server-side enforcement

questions.title: Replacing a Row-Counting Loop With GlideAggregate
questions.prompt: The following script loops through every open Priority 1 incident just to print a count. Rewrite it so the database does the counting instead of the script.
questions.modelAnswer: Replace the GlideRecord loop with GlideAggregate, which asks the database to compute COUNT directly and never retrieves full row data at all: build the same addQuery filters, call addAggregate('COUNT'), run .query(), and read the result with getAggregate('COUNT') after a single .next(). This turns a query that fetches every matching row just to increment a counter into a query that returns one number.
questions.professionalAnswer: Any time I see while (gr.next()) { count++; }, I treat it as a GlideAggregate waiting to happen. There's no reason to pull full row data across the network for every Priority 1 incident just to throw it away and keep an integer -- GlideAggregate does the counting at the database layer and hands back only the number I actually need.
commonMistakes: Looping a full GlideRecord result just to increment a counter
Not knowing GlideAggregate is a separate, dedicated API for COUNT/SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX
Forgetting to call .next() once before reading getAggregate() on a GlideAggregate result
keyPoints: GlideAggregate never retrieves full row data, only the computed aggregate
addAggregate('COUNT') plus getAggregate('COUNT') replaces a manual counting loop
The same addQuery filters apply identically to GlideAggregate
Any 'loop and increment' pattern is a signal GlideAggregate should be used instead

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rewrites the script using GlideAggregate
Correctly applies the same query filters
Explains why this avoids pulling full row data

questions.title: Diagnosing a Production Instance That 'Feels Slow Everywhere' After a Deploy
questions.prompt: The morning after a scoped application deployment, users across multiple unrelated departments report the instance 'feels slow' -- form saves lag, and some pages time out. Nothing in the deployment touched performance-critical code on paper. Walk through how you'd diagnose this, given that the real cause could be a recursive Business Rule, an N+1 query newly introduced, semaphore exhaustion, or some combination.

deepDive.heading: Don't trust 'nothing touched performance'
deepDive.content: Low-code customization -- a Business Rule, a Client Script, a UI Policy -- rarely looks performance-related by inspection, and that's exactly why it's the most common real cause of this symptom. A Business Rule added to fix one field's default value can run on every insert to that table, far outside the scope anyone was thinking about when they wrote it. Start from the assumption that the deployment is the most likely cause until profiling data says otherwise, rather than ruling it out because it 'looks like' a small, safe change.

deepDive.heading: Check the debug/profiler signature for recursion first
deepDive.content: Turn on Debug Business Rule and reproduce a single, representative save on an affected table. If the same business rule name appears multiple times for one user action, with durations often trending toward zero, that's the signature of a recursive trigger -- usually current.update() called inside an update-triggered rule with no setWorkflow(false) guard. This is cheap to check and rules in or out one entire category fast.

deepDive.heading: Check for new query-in-loop patterns
deepDive.content: If recursion isn't the culprit, pull a Slow Request Log entry or a profiled transaction for an affected page and look for the same query (same table, same condition shape) repeated many times with an execution count attached, rather than running once. That repetition, not any single query's duration, is the tell that a query got left inside a loop in the new deployment's code -- a classic N+1 pattern introduced by a Business Rule or Script Include that re-queries a related table per row instead of dot-walking or querying once outside the loop.

deepDive.heading: Rule out semaphore exhaustion as a compounding factor
deepDive.content: If individual scripts actually profile fast but requests still feel slow platform-wide, check whether a category of work -- background jobs, a specific transaction type -- is saturating its semaphore pool on one or more nodes. A request waiting in queue for a free slot looks exactly like generic slowness to the end user even though the request itself would run in under a second if it could start immediately. If the new deployment introduced heavy scheduled or background processing, it may be consuming a shared pool other transaction types also depend on.

deepDive.heading: Converging on the real root cause
deepDive.content: The diagnostic order matters: recursion and query-in-loop are both relatively cheap, fast checks with unambiguous profiler signatures, so check those first. Semaphore exhaustion requires looking at node-level health rather than one transaction's script trace, so it's the next layer once script-level causes are ruled out or fixed. Confirm a fix by repeating the exact same reproduction step and watching the signature disappear from the debug panel or profiler.

deepDive.heading: Why this is rarely just one cause
deepDive.content: In a real scoped application deployment, these causes compound rather than existing in isolation: an N+1 query makes each affected transaction slower and longer-running, which means it occupies a semaphore slot longer, which increases the odds of that pool saturating under normal load -- turning a script-level inefficiency into a platform-wide symptom that looks, to the end user, indistinguishable from any other cause on this list. Fixing only one may partially help without resolving the full symptom.

keyPoints: Low-code customization is the most common real cause, even when it 'looks' safe
The debug panel's recursion signature is a repeated rule name with shrinking durations
A profiler's execution count, not duration, reveals a query stuck in a loop
Semaphore exhaustion makes a fast script look slow because it's queued, not because it's slow
These causes often compound rather than acting independently
commonMistakes: Ruling out the recent deployment because the code 'doesn't look' performance-related
Treating a slow transaction as a slow script without checking whether it was actually queued
Fixing only the first cause found instead of checking whether multiple causes are compounding

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Checks the recursion signature in the debug panel before anything else
Correctly diagnoses a query-in-loop pattern using execution count
Correctly rules semaphore exhaustion in or out using queue-vs-execution reasoning

questions.title: Reading a Profiler Line That Says 'problem [47 executions] -- 2980 ms'
questions.prompt: A debug panel for one transaction shows the same problem table query repeated 47 times, each one small. Before opening a line of code, what does the execution count alone tell you about where the query sits, and what's the fix once you confirm it?
questions.modelAnswer: An execution count of 47 for the exact same query shape is the signature of a query sitting inside a loop over roughly 47 outer rows -- nobody writes code that intentionally queries problem 47 times in one transaction, so that number alone tells you to go looking for a while loop with a fresh GlideRecord query against problem inside it, almost certainly re-querying a related record one at a time instead of dot-walking an existing reference field. The fix is dot-walking the reference field already sitting on the outer record (for example incGr.problem_id.number) instead of opening a brand-new GlideRecord and running a fresh query for every iteration, which collapses the 47 repeated queries down to zero additional ones.
questions.professionalAnswer: The execution count is the whole diagnosis before I even open the script -- 47 executions of the identical query shape means there's a loop with roughly 47 iterations and a query inside it, full stop. I go straight to looking for the field that's being re-queried and check whether it's already a reference field on the record I'm already looping over; almost always it is, and dot-walking it eliminates every one of those 47 queries without changing the output at all.

Not recognizing a high execution count as the signature of a query-in-a-loop pattern
Opening a new GlideRecord to re-query a related table instead of dot-walking an existing reference field
keyPoints: A repeated execution count, not duration, is the signature of a query stuck in a loop
The count roughly matches the outer loop's row count
Dot-walking a reference field already on the record avoids the extra query entirely
The fix produces identical output with zero additional queries

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly interprets the execution count as a query-in-loop signature
Proposes dot-walking as the correct fix

questions.title: A Request Takes 8 Seconds But the Script Runs in Under 1 -- Why?
questions.prompt: You profile a slow transaction and the actual script logic completes in well under a second, yet the end user waited 8 seconds. Explain how semaphore exhaustion produces exactly this symptom, and why optimizing the script further would be the wrong fix.
questions.modelAnswer: A semaphore is a per-node concurrency limit on how many requests of a given category can run simultaneously, and when every slot in that category's pool is busy, a new request of the same type has to queue and wait for a slot to free up before it even starts running. From the user's point of view that wait is indistinguishable from the script itself being slow, but the script never actually ran for 8 seconds -- it ran for under a second once it finally got a slot, after sitting in queue for the rest of the time. Optimizing the script further is the wrong fix because the script was never the bottleneck; the fix has to target the contention itself -- understanding which category of work is saturating the pool and why so much of it is piling up at once.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd stop looking at the script the moment the profiled execution time doesn't match the user-perceived wait -- that gap is the tell. Semaphore exhaustion means the request spent most of its time in a queue, not in execution, because every slot in its pool was already busy. Shaving milliseconds off a script that already runs in under a second does nothing for a problem that's actually about too much of some other category of work saturating a shared, limited pool.
commonMistakes: Assuming a slow-feeling request always means a slow script
Trying to optimize a script that already profiles fast
Not distinguishing queue-wait time from actual execution time
keyPoints: A semaphore limits how many requests of a category run simultaneously, per node
Semaphore exhaustion means new requests of that type queue for a free slot
Queue-wait looks identical to slowness from the end user's perspective
The real fix targets contention on the saturated pool, not the script itself

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a semaphore is and how exhaustion happens
Correctly explains why this looks like slowness to the end user
Explains why script optimization would miss the real cause

questions.title: A Flow Step References a Record That Was Deleted Three Steps Earlier
questions.prompt: A flow triggers on record creation, and a later step silently fails to apply logic because a data pill resolves to nothing. Diagnose the likely cause and explain exactly where you'd look to confirm it.
questions.modelAnswer: The likely cause is a timing or record-lifecycle problem: the flow references a related record through a data pill, and that related record was deleted between the trigger firing and the later step actually executing. The pill doesn't error -- it just silently resolves to null, and any logic depending on it behaves unpredictably. Confirm this by opening the execution log for that specific run, finding the step in question, and looking at what the pill actually held at that moment, rather than assuming the field 'should' have had a value.
questions.professionalAnswer: I never assume a null pill means the pill is broken -- I go straight to the execution log for that run and look at the exact value the pill resolved to at that step. Nine times out of ten it's exactly this: something changed the state of a related record between the trigger and that step running, and the pill is accurately reporting that the thing it pointed to no longer exists in the state the flow expected.
commonMistakes: Assuming a null data pill means the pill itself is misconfigured rather than a timing issue
Not checking the execution log for the specific run in question
Assuming the field 'should' have a value instead of verifying what it actually held at that moment

The record a pill references can change or be deleted between trigger and later steps
The execution log shows exactly what a pill held at the moment a step ran

questions.title: A Flow Is 'Just Stuck' at an Approval Step
questions.prompt: An approval-gated flow has been sitting in a waiting state for two days with no error. Diagnose the most likely real cause and explain why this isn't a bug in the traditional sense.
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely cause is that the approval was routed to the wrong person or an empty group, so the flow is genuinely waiting for a response that will never come because nobody was actually notified -- the execution log will show the run as 'waiting' at the approval step, and inspecting the resolved approver or group pill will reveal it's empty or points to someone who was never meant to approve this. This isn't a bug in the traditional sense because the flow is working exactly as designed; it's correctly waiting on a real approval decision, it's just waiting on the wrong recipient.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I assume anything is broken, I check the execution log and look at the resolved approver or group pill on that specific approval step -- 'stuck' almost always means 'waiting on an empty or wrong recipient,' not 'the flow engine is malfunctioning.' The flow did exactly what it was built to do; the actual problem is upstream, in whatever logic resolved who should approve this.

Not checking the resolved approver/group pill's actual value
Treating the symptom (waiting) as the problem instead of the routing that caused it

The execution log shows the run as 'waiting' at the approval step
Inspecting the resolved approver/group pill reveals the real misconfiguration
The flow is behaving correctly; the upstream routing logic is the actual problem

Correctly identifies how to confirm it via the execution log and pill values
Explains why this isn't a flow engine bug
